title: The Firstborn, the Feast, and the Pillar
summary: The LORD claims every firstborn in Israel as his own, and Moses tells the people to remember the day of their release by keeping the Feast of Unleavened Bread and by redeeming their firstborn sons, explaining both to their children. Then Israel sets out, not by the short road along the coast but toward the wilderness and the Red Sea, carrying Joseph's bones. The LORD goes before them in a pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night.
story: Israel has just walked out of Egypt. In chapter 12 the LORD struck down the firstborn of Egypt, passed over the Israelite houses marked with the blood of the Passover lamb, and Pharaoh finally let the people go. Before the story moves on, this chapter pauses to make sure the night will never be forgotten. The firstborn of Israel were spared when Egypt's died, so from now on they belong to the LORD in a special way. Then the march begins, and the chapter introduces two things that will shape the rest of Exodus and Numbers: the wilderness route and the pillar of God's presence. Joseph's bones, carried out of Egypt, tie this departure back to the end of Genesis, where Joseph foresaw that God would bring the family home (Genesis 50:24-25). The chapter ends with Israel camped on the edge of the wilderness, heading toward the sea where the next great act will happen.
historical:
The date of the exodus is debated. One view, based on 1 Kings 6:1, which places it 480 years before Solomon began the temple, puts it in the fifteenth century BC. Another, pointing to the store city of Rameses (Exodus 1:11) and to evidence of settlement in Canaan, prefers the thirteenth century BC, in the reign of Ramesses II. Other scholars see the account as a later telling of a smaller or more complex set of events. Readers of every view agree on the geography the chapter assumes: the eastern Nile Delta, and beyond it the Sinai region.

The "road through the land of the Philistines" was the main coastal route from Egypt to Canaan, the shortest way. In the New Kingdom period Egypt guarded that road with a chain of fortresses, so a column of runaway slaves would have met soldiers. The mention of the Philistines, who settled on that coast around the twelfth century BC, is taken by some as a later writer naming the route by what it was called in his own day, and by others as evidence for a later date. Succoth is often identified with a site in the Wadi Tumilat, a valley leading east from the Delta; Etham's location is unknown. The "Red Sea" of verse 18 translates the Hebrew yam suph, literally sea of reeds, and where Israel crossed is discussed at chapter 14.
cultural:
Two customs are set up here. The first is the redemption of the firstborn. Across the ancient Near East the firstborn son held a special place as heir, and firstborn animals and first fruits were often offered to the gods. Israel's law claims every firstborn for the LORD but refuses child sacrifice: sons are to be redeemed, bought back. Later law set the price at five shekels (Numbers 18:16) and gave the Levites to the LORD in place of the firstborn of all Israel (Numbers 3:11-13). The donkey, which was not a sacrificial animal, was redeemed with a lamb, or else killed rather than kept.

The second custom is teaching by ritual. The Feast of Unleavened Bread was a week-long festival in the month of Abib (a name connected with ripening ears of grain; it falls in the spring and was later called Nisan), and it is joined to the question a child asks: "What does this mean?" The sign "on your hand" and "on your forehead" may have been meant figuratively, like a string on the finger, but Jewish tradition came to apply it literally in tefillin (phylacteries), small leather boxes containing Scripture passages, including parts of this chapter, bound on the arm and head during prayer. Examples of them were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, and Jesus mentions them in Matthew 23:5.
literary: The chapter has two halves. Verses 1-16 are instruction, set in Moses' voice and addressed to future generations who will live in the land; they alternate between the feast (verses 3-10) and the firstborn (verses 11-16), and each section closes with nearly the same line about a sign on the hand and the forehead and the LORD's "mighty hand". Verses 17-22 are narrative, and they bring the story back to the road. The repeated phrases "out of the house of slavery" and "with a mighty hand" are the chapter's refrain, a short creed Israel was meant to say aloud. The fatherly speech in verses 8 and 14-15 is striking: the adult is told to say "what the LORD did for me", so that every generation speaks as if it had come out of Egypt itself.

outline.t: Remember the day: the Feast of Unleavened Bread
Redeeming the firstborn and teaching the children
The long way round, with Joseph's bones
The pillar of cloud and fire

doctrines.note: The firstborn sons of Israel live because they were spared, and they are to be redeemed at a price. The chapter sets up a basic biblical idea: a life that belongs to God is bought back by a substitute or payment.
God chooses the longer road because he knows the people's weakness, and he leads them himself, day and night. His guidance is not only rescue from danger but care for what his people can bear.
The faith is to be passed on in the home, through practice and through answering children's questions. Each generation is taught to tell the exodus as its own story.

words.note: Padah, to ransom or redeem, to set free by payment. It is used for buying back the firstborn and elsewhere for God's rescue of Israel from Egypt (Deuteronomy 7:8). The idea behind it shapes the New Testament's language of redemption.

Peter, that which opens (the womb), the firstborn. Along with the ordinary word for firstborn (bekhor, H1060), it marks the chapter's claim: the first life that comes from a mother, human or animal, belongs to the LORD.

Zikkaron, a memorial or reminder. The feast and its signs are meant to keep memory alive. In the Bible, remembering is active: it shapes how people live, and it is sustained by repeated practice rather than a single recollection.

Ammud, pillar or column. The pillar of cloud and fire becomes the visible sign of God's presence leading Israel through the wilderness, and later it stands at the entrance of the tent of meeting (33:9). It is guidance and presence at once.

christ: Luke tells how Mary and Joseph brought the infant Jesus to the temple "to present Him to the Lord", and he cites this chapter's law that every firstborn male is to be consecrated to the Lord (Luke 2:22-23). Jesus, the firstborn of his mother, is redeemed as the law required. The New Testament then turns the image around: Paul calls Christ "the firstborn over all creation" and "firstborn from among the dead" (Colossians 1:15, 18), and Peter says believers were redeemed not with silver or gold but with the precious blood of Christ (1 Peter 1:18-19). The firstborn who was bought back becomes the one who pays the ransom for others. The pillar of cloud and fire also points forward, thematically rather than by prediction, to God's presence dwelling among his people, which John says came to its fullness when "the Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us" (John 1:14).

hard.q: Why does God claim the firstborn, and what about the firstborn of Egypt who died?
hard.a: The claim on Israel's firstborn follows directly from the death of Egypt's firstborn in chapter 12, and a reader can feel the weight of that. The text presents the plague as judgment on a regime that had enslaved Israel and ordered the killing of its baby boys (1:22), and as the climax of a long contest in which Pharaoh repeatedly refused to let the people go. The law here draws a lesson for Israel: its firstborn are alive by mercy, not by merit, and so they belong to God. Notice that the chapter rules out the pagan answer to such a claim. The LORD does not take Israel's children in sacrifice; he requires that they be redeemed. Readers still differ on how to weigh the deaths in Egypt, whether as the just judgment of God on a nation's cruelty, as a hard element in an ancient account written in the idiom of its day, or in some combination, and the Bible itself treats the matter with seriousness rather than triumph.

questions: Israel was told to tell the exodus as "what the LORD did for me". What story of God's faithfulness do you want the next generation to hear from you?
God led Israel the long way because they might turn back at the first sign of war. Where might a longer road in your life be a form of care?
Rituals like the feast were meant to keep memory alive. What practices help you remember what God has done, and which have gone dry?
